pharm: Caloric agent / fluid and electrolyte replenisher / antihypoglycemic
quick: Hypoglycemia: 25 g (50 mL D50W) IV; maintenance fluid: D5W titrated to needs
Acceptable when indicated; avoid maternal hyperglycemia near delivery
No specific adjustment; monitor fluid/electrolyte and glucose balance
Caution; monitor glucose, give carefully in hepatic failure
Give thiamine before/with dextrose in alcohol use to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Blood glucose, serum electrolytes (Na, K, phosphate), fluid status
summary: Dextrose (D-glucose) injection is a carbohydrate source used to supply calories and free water, treat hypoglycemia, and serve as a vehicle/diluent. Concentrations range from D5W (5%) for fluid and calories, through D10/D25, to D50W (50%) for acute hypoglycemia. Concentrated solutions (>5% or osmolarity >=900 mOsm/L) require central venous administration. Dextrose is oxidized to carbon dioxide and water, yielding ~3.4 kcal per gram.
indications: Source of calories and fluid replenishment (parenteral nutrition admixtures, maintenance fluids)
Source of water and calories when oral intake is restricted
Adjunct in management of hyperkalemia (with insulin)

dosage.d: 10-25 g IV (e.g., 20-50 mL of D50W) bolus
dosage.n: Recheck glucose in 10-15 min; follow with continuous infusion or oral intake

dosage.d: 0.5-1 g/kg IV (2-4 mL/kg D25W in children; 5-10 mL/kg D10W in neonates)
dosage.n: Avoid D50W in young children due to osmolarity/vein injury

dosage.d: D5W or D5/saline titrated to fluid and caloric needs
dosage.n: Typical glucose oxidation limit ~4-5 mg/kg/min; avoid overfeeding

dosage.d: Concentrated dextrose (e.g., 50-70%) diluted in PN with amino acids/lipids
dosage.n: Individualize to clinical condition, weight and nutritional needs

dosage.d: 25 g dextrose IV with 10 units regular insulin
dosage.n: Drives potassium intracellularly; monitor glucose to avoid hypoglycemia

admin: Solutions >5% dextrose or osmolarity >=~900 mOsm/L (e.g., D10 and above) must be given through a central vein; <=5% may go peripherally
Pharmacy bulk packages (e.g., 70%) are for admixture only - NOT for direct IV infusion
Inspect for particulate matter and clarity; do not use if precipitate present (pulmonary embolism risk)
Discontinue concentrated dextrose infusions gradually to avoid rebound hypoglycemia
Use a dedicated line or verify compatibility; do not administer through the same set as blood
In patients at risk (alcohol use, malnutrition) give thiamine before/with dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
moa: Dextrose provides glucose, the body's primary metabolic fuel. Infused glucose is taken up by cells and oxidized via glycolysis and the citric acid cycle to carbon dioxide and water, yielding approximately 3.4 kcal per gram (hydrous). It raises blood glucose to correct hypoglycemia, supplies caloric substrate, and provides free water (when metabolized) for hydration.

absolute: Severe dehydration (hypertonic dextrose worsens hyperosmolar state)
Clinically significant hyperglycemia not yet controlled
relative: Risk of refeeding syndrome (severe malnutrition, prolonged fasting)
Hepatic failure with impaired glucose handling
monitor: Patients on insulin or oral hypoglycemics
Patients at risk of thiamine deficiency (alcoholism, malnutrition)
Neonates and preterm infants (aluminum toxicity, glucose lability)
Patients with cardiac or renal impairment (fluid status)

preg: Appropriate administration during pregnancy is not expected to cause adverse developmental outcomes. However, maternal hyperglycemia from glucose-containing fluids near delivery has been associated with neonatal hypoglycemia. Monitor maternal glucose, particularly intrapartum.
lact: Dextrose injection is compatible with breastfeeding; glucose is a normal physiologic substrate and is not expected to harm a breastfed infant.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for dextrose itself, but monitor fluid balance, electrolytes and glucose carefully. Patients with impaired renal function are at higher risk of aluminum accumulation from parenteral solutions and of fluid overload.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic failure where glucose metabolism may be impaired, increasing the risk of hyperglycemia and lactic acidosis. Monitor blood glucose, liver function and ammonia, particularly with prolonged parenteral nutrition.

major: Insulin and oral hypoglycemics - opposing/modifying effect on blood glucose; dosing must be coordinated
moderate: Diuretics and other fluids - additive effects on fluid/electrolyte balance
minor: Drugs incompatible with dextrose solutions (e.g., certain antibiotics, blood products) - check compatibility before co-administration
interactions.alcohol: In chronic alcohol use, administer thiamine before or with dextrose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.
interactions.diagnostics: Raises measured blood glucose; can transiently affect electrolyte (potassium, phosphate, sodium) and acid-base measurements.

serious: Vein damage and thrombosis (concentrated solutions peripherally)
emergency: Severe dilutional hyponatremia with cerebral edema

monitoring: Blood glucose, especially in diabetics, neonates, and with concentrated infusions
Serum electrolytes including sodium, potassium and phosphate
Fluid status and signs of fluid overload (edema, pulmonary congestion)
Acid-base status with high-rate or prolonged infusion
Liver function and ammonia with long-term parenteral nutrition
Infusion site for phlebitis or extravasation
counsel: This is given by infusion in a healthcare setting; report pain, swelling or redness at the IV site
Tell staff if you have diabetes, kidney, heart or liver problems
Expect periodic blood glucose and electrolyte checks during treatment
Report symptoms such as excessive thirst, confusion, swelling, or shortness of breath
If you have a history of heavy alcohol use, ensure thiamine has been given
pk: Immediate rise in blood glucose with IV bolus
Peak glucose within minutes of bolus administration
Rapidly metabolized; glucose cleared per metabolic demand (no fixed half-life)
Transient after bolus (minutes); sustained with continuous infusion
Store at room temperature ~20-25 C (68-77 F); do not freeze; avoid excessive heat
pearls: Each gram of hydrous dextrose provides ~3.4 kcal
D50W (50%) is the standard adult ampoule for acute hypoglycemia (25 g per 50 mL); use lower concentrations (D10/D25) in children to avoid vein injury
Solutions >5% or >=~900 mOsm/L must be infused centrally to avoid phlebitis and thrombosis
Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Pharmacy bulk packages (50-70%) are for admixture only and are NOT for direct infusion
D5W is effectively free water once glucose is metabolized - watch for dilutional hyponatremia
missed: Not applicable - dextrose is administered by infusion or bolus under medical supervision rather than on a fixed self-administered schedule.
overdose: Excessive infusion rate or concentration causes hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, glycosuria, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance; severe dilutional hyponatremia and severe hyperglycemia can be fatal. Discontinue the infusion and institute corrective measures, including exogenous insulin for hyperglycemia and management of fluid/electrolyte and acid-base imbalance, with attention to CNS, respiratory and cardiovascular status.
